paths.title: Agentic Design Patterns Academy
paths.attribution: Based on 'Agentic Design Patterns: A Hands-On Guide to Building Intelligent Systems' by Antonio Gulli. Original transformed teaching content; the author donates royalties to Save the Children.
paths.description: Master 21 agentic design patterns by building, debugging, and applying each one.
paths.tagline: Build, debug and apply the 21 patterns that power real AI agents.

chapters.title: 1. Prompt Chaining
chapters.tagline: Prompt Chaining = An assembly line
objectives: Big tasks that one prompt does badly — break them into ordered steps where each output feeds the next.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Prompt Chaining = An assembly line
payload.why_it_matters: Big tasks that one prompt does badly — break them into ordered steps where each output feeds the next.
objectives: Use when: A task has clear sequential stages; Each stage needs a focused instruction
Avoid when: The task is a single simple ask; Stages are independent (use Parallelization)
Example: Summarize a doc → extract the action items → format them as JSON.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Output of each step is the input of the next
Each link has one job and one clear format
A broken link breaks the chain — validate between steps
payload.mistake: Letting step 1's messy output flow into step 2 without a defined structure.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: You must turn a long meeting transcript into a clean JSON list of decisions with owners and dates.

options.feedback: Right — sequential stages, each feeding the next, with a structured final step.
These steps depend on each other; you can't extract before you summarize.
There's only one task type here, nothing to route.

missions.title: Build Lab
missions.objective: Assemble a content pipeline that turns a raw document into validated JSON.

payload.goal: Assemble a content pipeline that turns a raw document into validated JSON.
payload.prompt: Tap the steps in the correct order to build the chain.
payload.success: Summarize → Extract → Format. Each step feeds the next; the last one enforces structure.

missions.title: Broken Agent Fix
missions.objective: Diagnose the failure and choose the fix.

payload.scenario: An agent pipeline outputs free text instead of the JSON the next system needs.
payload.broken: step3 = 'Write a nice summary of the items.'
options: Add an explicit output-format/schema instruction and a validation step
Raise the temperature so it's more creative
payload.explain: The final link must declare its schema and validate — otherwise downstream parsing breaks.

missions.title: Boss: Prompt Chaining
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.q: In a chain, what makes a link reliable?
options: Its output has a defined, validated structure
questions.explain: Defined I/O contracts between steps keep the chain from drifting.

questions.q: A 3-stage pipeline keeps producing malformed final JSON. Best fix?
options: Merge all steps into one prompt
Add a validate/format step and reject malformed intermediate output
questions.explain: Validation between links catches errors before they cascade.

recap: Output of each step is the input of the next
Each link has one job and one clear format
A broken link breaks the chain — validate between steps

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Prompt Chaining solve?
review_cards.answer: It breaks a complex task into ordered steps, each output feeding the next.

review_cards.prompt: When should you NOT use Prompt Chaining?
review_cards.answer: When the task is a single simple ask, or when subtasks are independent (use Parallelization).
Unstructured output from one step corrupts the next — links must have defined I/O.

review_cards.prompt: Pattern often confused with Prompt Chaining?
review_cards.answer: Parallelization — but chaining is sequential & dependent, parallelization is independent.

review_cards.prompt: What should you validate in a chain?
review_cards.answer: The structure of each intermediate output before it feeds the next step.
Transcript → summary → action-item extraction → formatted JSON.

chapters.title: 2. Routing
chapters.tagline: Routing = A traffic controller
objectives: Many possible request types — send each to the specialist best equipped to handle it.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Routing = A traffic controller
payload.why_it_matters: Many possible request types — send each to the specialist best equipped to handle it.
objectives: Use when: Requests fall into distinct categories; Different handlers/tools fit different intents
Avoid when: Every request is the same kind; There's only one capable handler
Example: A support message could be billing, technical, or cancellation — route to the right agent.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Map each intent to a specialist
payload.mistake: No fallback route, so unknown intents crash or get mishandled.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: A customer request could be billing, technical support, or a cancellation.

options.feedback: Right — classify intent, dispatch to the matching specialist, with a fallback.
Chaining runs fixed stages; it can't pick between different handlers.
Retrieval helps answer, but doesn't decide which department handles the request.

missions.title: Boss: Routing
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

options: A fallback/default route for unknown intents
questions.explain: Unclassified intents need a safe default instead of failing.

questions.q: A router sends refunds to the FAQ bot. Root cause?
options: The FAQ bot is too smart
questions.explain: Routing quality depends on accurate intent detection.

recap: Map each intent to a specialist

review_cards.answer: Directing each request to the specialist handler best suited to its intent.
When all requests are the same kind or only one handler exists.
No fallback route, or misclassified intent sending work to the wrong handler.

review_cards.prompt: What must a router always have?
review_cards.answer: A default/fallback route for unknown or low-confidence intents.
Prompt Chaining — but chaining is fixed stages, routing chooses among handlers.
Triaging a support request into billing / technical / cancellation.

chapters.title: 3. Parallelization
chapters.tagline: Parallelization = A task swarm
objectives: Independent subtasks that waste time if run one-by-one — fan them out, then merge.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Parallelization = A task swarm
payload.why_it_matters: Independent subtasks that waste time if run one-by-one — fan them out, then merge.
objectives: Use when: Subtasks don't depend on each other; Latency matters
Avoid when: Steps depend on previous output (use Chaining); Order matters
Example: Research 5 competitors at once, then merge into one comparison table.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Merge results into one coherent answer
payload.mistake: Parallelizing dependent steps, so later tasks use stale/missing inputs.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: You need to gather facts about 6 unrelated companies and combine them into a report.

options.feedback: Right — independent lookups fan out, then a merge step combines them.
These lookups don't depend on each other — chaining would be needlessly slow.
Reflection improves one answer; it doesn't gather parallel data.

missions.title: Boss: Parallelization
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.explain: Independence is what makes concurrency safe.

questions.q: What step is essential after fan-out?
questions.explain: Results must be combined coherently.

recap: Merge results into one coherent answer

review_cards.answer: Running independent subtasks concurrently to cut latency, then merging results.
When steps depend on each other or order matters — use Prompt Chaining.
Parallelizing dependent steps so later work uses missing/stale inputs.
A merge/aggregation step that combines the parallel results.
Prompt Chaining — chaining is dependent & sequential.
Researching multiple sources at once and merging into one report.

chapters.title: 4. Reflection
chapters.tagline: Reflection = A self-review loop
objectives: First drafts are often wrong — have the agent critique and improve its own output.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Reflection = A self-review loop
payload.why_it_matters: First drafts are often wrong — have the agent critique and improve its own output.
objectives: Use when: Quality matters more than speed; Errors are catchable by self-review
Avoid when: Latency/cost is critical; The task is trivial
Example: Draft an answer → critique it for gaps → produce an improved version.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Revise to fix the identified weaknesses
payload.mistake: A critique step that rubber-stamps the draft without finding real weaknesses.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: An agent's first-pass code reviews keep missing edge cases.

options.feedback: Right — add a critique-then-revise loop to catch what the first pass missed.
There's one task; nothing to route.
Running more copies in parallel won't add self-critique.

missions.title: Boss: Reflection
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

options: identify at least one concrete weakness
questions.explain: Reflection that finds nothing adds no value.
Self-review costs time but improves results.

recap: Revise to fix the identified weaknesses

review_cards.answer: Improving output quality by having the agent critique and revise its own work.
When latency/cost is critical or the task is trivial.
A critique that rubber-stamps the draft without finding real weaknesses.

review_cards.prompt: What must the critique step do?
review_cards.answer: Identify at least one concrete weakness to fix.
More latency/cost in exchange for higher quality.
Draft → self-critique for gaps → improved final answer.

chapters.title: 5. Tool Use
chapters.tagline: Tool Use = An agent reaching outside itself
objectives: LLMs can't reliably compute, fetch live data, or act — give them tools and let them decide when to call.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Tool Use = An agent reaching outside itself
payload.why_it_matters: LLMs can't reliably compute, fetch live data, or act — give them tools and let them decide when to call.
objectives: Use when: You need exact math, live data, or real actions; The model alone would hallucinate the answer
Avoid when: The model already knows reliably; A tool call adds risk with no benefit
Example: Use a calculator for exact arithmetic instead of trusting token prediction.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Decide IF a tool is needed
Pick the RIGHT tool and arguments
Feed the result back into the answer
payload.mistake: Calling tools unnecessarily, or ignoring/failing to incorporate the tool's result.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: The agent must answer 'What's 18.5% of $2,430?' but keeps inventing numbers.

options.feedback: Right — offload exact arithmetic to a calculator tool and use its result.
Self-critique won't make token prediction good at exact math.
Remembering won't compute the number reliably.

missions.title: Build Lab
missions.objective: Equip an agent that answers exact financial questions safely.

payload.goal: Equip an agent that answers exact financial questions safely.
payload.prompt: Select ONLY the components this agent truly needs.

blocks.label: Step that uses the tool's result

payload.success: Calculator + a step that uses its output + a confirmation gate. The image generator and mass-mailer are needless risk.

missions.title: Broken Agent Fix
missions.objective: Diagnose the failure and choose the fix.

payload.scenario: An agent calls a web-search tool for every message, even 'hello', burning cost and adding latency.
payload.broken: policy = always call web_search before replying
options: Call the tool only when the query actually needs external/live info
payload.explain: Tool use should be conditional on need — not a reflex on every turn.

missions.title: Boss: Tool Use
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.q: When should an agent call a tool?
options: Only when the model can't reliably do it alone
questions.explain: Tools add capability AND risk — call them with purpose.

questions.q: After a tool returns, the agent must…
options: incorporate the result into its answer
questions.explain: An unused tool result is wasted (or unsafe).

recap: Decide IF a tool is needed
Pick the RIGHT tool and arguments
Feed the result back into the answer

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Tool Use solve?
review_cards.answer: Lets an agent compute, fetch live data, or act by calling external functions instead of guessing.

review_cards.prompt: When NOT to use a tool?
review_cards.answer: When the model already knows reliably, or the call adds risk with no benefit.
Unnecessary calls, wrong tool/args, or ignoring the returned result.

review_cards.prompt: What must happen after a tool runs?
review_cards.answer: The result must be incorporated into the agent's response.
Tools can take real actions — gate risky ones behind confirmation.
Calling a calculator for exact math or an API for live prices.

chapters.title: 6. Planning
chapters.tagline: Planning = A map before the journey
objectives: Multi-step goals where acting blindly fails — make a plan, then execute and track it.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Planning = A map before the journey
payload.why_it_matters: Multi-step goals where acting blindly fails — make a plan, then execute and track it.
objectives: Use when: The goal needs several coordinated steps; You want to track progress and adapt
Avoid when: A single action solves it; The environment changes faster than you can plan
Example: Plan: gather data → analyze → draft → review → publish, executing each in order.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Decompose the goal into ordered steps
Track state and re-plan on failure
payload.mistake: Making a plan but never tracking execution state, so the agent repeats or skips steps.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: An agent must organize a multi-step product launch with dependencies.

options.feedback: Right — decompose into ordered steps, execute, and track state.
There are dependencies, so pure fan-out would break order.
Tools help execute steps, but you still need a plan to sequence them.

missions.title: Boss: Planning
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.explain: State tracking prevents repeats/skips and enables re-planning.

questions.q: When a step fails, the planner should…
questions.explain: Adaptation on failure is core to planning.

recap: Decompose the goal into ordered steps
Track state and re-plan on failure

review_cards.answer: Coordinating multi-step goals by decomposing, executing, and tracking progress.
When one action solves it, or the world changes faster than plans hold.
No execution-state tracking — the agent repeats or skips steps.

review_cards.prompt: What should a planner do on failure?
review_cards.answer: Re-plan or trigger a fallback.
Plain Tool Use — tools execute steps, planning sequences them.
An agent sequencing gather → analyze → draft → review → publish.

chapters.title: 7. Multi-Agent Collaboration
chapters.tagline: Multi-Agent Collaboration = A specialist team
objectives: One generalist agent struggles with complex work — split roles across specialists that collaborate.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Multi-Agent Collaboration = A specialist team
payload.why_it_matters: One generalist agent struggles with complex work — split roles across specialists that collaborate.
objectives: Use when: Work has distinct specialties; A coordinator can manage handoffs
Avoid when: A single agent suffices; Coordination overhead outweighs benefits
Example: Planner, researcher, builder, reviewer, and safety-checker agents working together.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

points: Give each agent a distinct role
payload.mistake: Unclear handoffs, so agents duplicate work or drop tasks between them.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: A complex report needs research, drafting, fact-checking, and a final safety review.

options.feedback: Right — distinct specialist roles with clear handoffs and a reviewer.
Reflection is one agent self-reviewing, not a team of specialists.
Routing picks ONE handler; this needs several working together.

missions.title: Boss: Multi-Agent Collaboration
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.explain: Role clarity + handoffs prevent dropped/duplicated work.

questions.q: Who guards quality in a team?
questions.explain: A coordinator or reviewer keeps the team aligned.

recap: Give each agent a distinct role

review_cards.answer: Splitting complex work across specialist agents that collaborate.
When one agent suffices or coordination overhead outweighs benefits.
Unclear handoffs causing duplicated or dropped tasks.

review_cards.prompt: What roles keep a team healthy?
review_cards.answer: Distinct specialists plus a coordinator/reviewer.
Reflection (one agent) and Routing (one handler) — multi-agent is a collaborating team.
Planner + researcher + builder + reviewer + safety checker.

chapters.title: 8. Memory Management
chapters.tagline: Memory Management = A durable notebook, not a hoarder's attic
objectives: Agents forget across turns or drown in irrelevant history — manage what to keep, summarize, and retrieve.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Memory Management = A durable notebook, not a hoarder's attic
payload.why_it_matters: Agents forget across turns or drown in irrelevant history — manage what to keep, summarize, and retrieve.
objectives: Use when: Multi-turn or long-running tasks; Context exceeds the window
Avoid when: Single-shot tasks; All context fits and stays relevant
Example: Summarize old turns and retrieve only the memories relevant to the current step.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

payload.metaphor: A durable notebook, not a hoarder's attic
payload.mistake: Dumping the entire history every call, or leaking private/irrelevant memory.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: A long-running assistant blows its context window by pasting all prior turns each call.

options.feedback: Right — summarize old turns and pull only relevant memories.
Running tasks in parallel doesn't fix context bloat.
Guardrails enforce safety, not context efficiency.

missions.title: Boss: Memory Management
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

options: Summarize old turns and retrieve by relevance
questions.explain: Selective memory beats raw history dumps.
Memory boundaries protect privacy and relevance.

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Memory Management solve?
review_cards.answer: Keeping relevant context across turns without overflowing the window or leaking noise.

review_cards.prompt: When NOT to manage memory heavily?
review_cards.answer: Single-shot tasks where all context fits and stays relevant.
Dumping full history every call, or leaking private/irrelevant memory.
Summarize older turns and retrieve only relevant memories.
Excluding private/irrelevant data from what you keep and retrieve.
A coding assistant summarizing earlier context and recalling only what's relevant now.

chapters.title: 9. Learning & Adaptation
chapters.tagline: Learning & Adaptation = An agent that gets better with practice
objectives: Static agents stagnate — capture feedback and outcomes to improve behavior over time.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Learning & Adaptation = An agent that gets better with practice
payload.why_it_matters: Static agents stagnate — capture feedback and outcomes to improve behavior over time.
objectives: Use when: Repeated tasks with feedback signals; Performance should improve with data
Avoid when: One-off tasks; No reliable feedback signal
Example: Log which answers users accepted and adapt future responses toward what works.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

payload.metaphor: An agent that gets better with practice
payload.mistake: Adapting on noisy or biased feedback, causing drift toward the wrong behavior.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: A recommendation agent should improve as it sees which suggestions users accept.

options.feedback: Right — capture feedback signals and adapt behavior over time.
Routing dispatches requests; it doesn't learn from outcomes.
Guardrails constrain; they don't improve performance from feedback.

missions.title: Boss: Learning & Adaptation
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.explain: Adaptation is only as good as its signal.
Bad signals push behavior the wrong way.

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Learning & Adaptation solve?
review_cards.answer: Improving agent behavior over time using feedback and outcomes.
One-off tasks or when no reliable feedback signal exists.
Adapting on noisy/biased feedback causing drift.
A reliable feedback/outcome signal.

review_cards.prompt: How to stay safe while adapting?
review_cards.answer: Guard against drift and validate changes.
Adapting recommendations from which suggestions users accept.

chapters.title: 10. Model Context Protocol (MCP)
chapters.tagline: Model Context Protocol (MCP) = A universal power outlet for tools
objectives: Every tool integration is bespoke — MCP is a standard way for agents to discover and call tools/data.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Model Context Protocol (MCP) = A universal power outlet for tools
payload.why_it_matters: Every tool integration is bespoke — MCP is a standard way for agents to discover and call tools/data.
objectives: Use when: You want portable, standardized tool/data access; Multiple agents share the same tools
Avoid when: A single hardcoded tool is enough; You need a one-off prototype
Example: An agent connects to an MCP server to use any registered tool without custom glue code.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

payload.metaphor: A universal power outlet for tools
points: A standard protocol, not a single API
payload.mistake: Treating MCP as 'just another API' and skipping its discovery/capability contract.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: You want many agents to share the same growing set of tools without rewriting integrations.

options.feedback: Right — a standard interface so tools are discoverable and portable.
Chaining sequences prompts; it doesn't standardize tool access.
Memory stores context, not a tool-integration standard.

missions.title: Boss: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

options: a standard protocol for tool/data access
questions.explain: MCP standardizes how agents discover and use capabilities.
Standardization removes bespoke glue per tool.

recap: A standard protocol, not a single API

review_cards.answer: Standardizing how agents discover and call tools/data, replacing bespoke integrations.
For a single hardcoded tool or a quick one-off prototype.
Treating it as just another API and ignoring its discovery/capability contract.
A universal, standardized 'outlet' so tools are plug-and-play across agents.
Plain Tool Use — MCP is the standard layer that makes tools portable.
Agents connecting to an MCP server to use any registered tool.

badge.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Adept
badge.description: Cleared the Model Context Protocol (MCP) chapter.

chapters.title: 11. Goal Setting & Monitoring
chapters.tagline: Goal Setting & Monitoring = A North Star with a progress dashboard
objectives: Agents wander without a clear objective — define goals and continuously check progress toward them.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Goal Setting & Monitoring = A North Star with a progress dashboard
payload.why_it_matters: Agents wander without a clear objective — define goals and continuously check progress toward them.
objectives: Use when: Long-running or autonomous tasks; Success must be measurable
Avoid when: Trivial single actions; No measurable success criteria
Example: Set 'reduce open tickets to <10' and monitor the count, adjusting actions until met.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

payload.metaphor: A North Star with a progress dashboard
payload.mistake: Vague goals with no success metric, so the agent never knows when it's done.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: An autonomous agent keeps working but never knows if it has succeeded.

options.feedback: Right — a measurable goal plus progress monitoring defines 'done'.
Tools execute actions; they don't define success.
Concurrency doesn't tell the agent when it's finished.

missions.title: Boss: Goal Setting & Monitoring
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.explain: Measurable goals create a clear finish line.

options: track progress and adjust toward the goal
questions.explain: Continuous checks keep work on target.

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Goal Setting solve?
review_cards.answer: Giving agents a measurable objective and tracking progress toward it.
Trivial single actions with no measurable success.
Vague goals with no success metric — the agent never knows it's done.
Concrete and measurable.
To track progress and adjust actions toward the goal.
Driving open tickets below a threshold and monitoring the count.

badge.title: Goal Setting & Monitoring Adept
badge.description: Cleared the Goal Setting & Monitoring chapter.

chapters.title: 12. Exception Handling & Recovery
chapters.tagline: Exception Handling & Recovery = Seatbelts and airbags
objectives: Tools fail, APIs time out, outputs malform — agents need defined failure paths, retries, and fallbacks.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Exception Handling & Recovery = Seatbelts and airbags
payload.why_it_matters: Tools fail, APIs time out, outputs malform — agents need defined failure paths, retries, and fallbacks.
objectives: Use when: Any production agent touching tools/APIs; Reliability matters
Avoid when: Throwaway demos (still risky); No external dependencies at all
Example: If a tool call fails, retry with backoff, then fall back to a safe default and inform the user.

missions.title: Mental Model
missions.objective: Lock in the visual metaphor.

payload.mistake: No fallback after an exception — the agent hangs, loops, or crashes silently.

missions.title: Pattern Selection Drill
missions.objective: Pick the right pattern — and learn why the others fall short.

rounds.scenario: An agent freezes whenever its search API times out.

options.feedback: Right — add retry-with-limit then a safe fallback path.
Self-critique doesn't handle infrastructure failures.
Ranking tasks won't recover from a timeout.

missions.title: Boss: Exception Handling & Recovery
missions.objective: Combine the ideas to clear the chapter.

questions.q: After an exception, an agent should…
options: retry within limits, then fall back safely
questions.explain: Bounded retries + fallback keep agents reliable.
Unbounded retries cause runaway behavior.

review_cards.prompt: What problem does Exception Handling solve?
review_cards.answer: Keeping agents reliable when tools/APIs fail via defined failure paths.
Any production agent with external dependencies.
No fallback after an error — the agent hangs, loops, or crashes silently.
A maximum attempt limit (and ideally backoff).
Retry within limits, then fall back to a safe default and report.
Falling back to cached data when a live API times out.

badge.title: Exception Handling & Recovery Adept
badge.description: Cleared the Exception Handling & Recovery chapter.

chapters.title: 13. Human-in-the-Loop
chapters.tagline: Human-in-the-Loop = A co-pilot asking before risky moves
objectives: Some actions are too risky for full autonomy — require human approval at key decision points.

missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

Irreversible or high-impact actions, or compliance needs.
Log the human decision and proceed accordingly.
An agent waiting for human sign-off before issuing a refund.

chapters.title: 14. Knowledge Retrieval (RAG)
chapters.tagline: Knowledge Retrieval (RAG) = Open-book, not from-memory
objectives: LLMs hallucinate facts they don't reliably know — retrieve real evidence first, then answer from it.

missions.title: Mission Brief
missions.objective: Get the pattern in 60 seconds before you build.

payload.tagline: Knowledge Retrieval (RAG) = Open-book, not from-memory
